title: "Join and transform polygons"
subtitle: "Real spatial work when the polygons start out in the table rather than in R"
---

## The spatial functions are on both sides of the line

The server has getting on for a hundred built-in `ST_` functions, so needing a spatial operation is not by itself a reason to bring data back. Buffers, intersections, transforms, areas and predicates all run where the data is.

That matters because the obvious chain of reasoning is wrong. Spatial work means `sf`, `sf` means R, R means collecting everything first: each step follows from the last and the conclusion is that geometry always crosses. It does not. You can put a spatial question to the server and get back a number.

Here is the shape, on the catchment polygons used throughout this guide. Four thousand polygons are read, unioned and measured, and one row comes back. Two connections are open because this page needs both: `con` runs the spatial work, and `acon` is the one that can carry raw geometry back, for the reason [Connect your R session to the data](connect.qmd) sets out.

The `st_` functions below are Databricks functions, not `sf` ones, even though several share a name. They are written inside an ordinary `dplyr` pipeline: `dbplyr` passes a function it does not recognise straight through to the server, so a spatial expression needs no translation to push down.

Worth being clear about what that means, because it is the one thing on this page that can mislead you. Inside a `dplyr` verb on a remote table, `st_area(g)` is not a call to `sf::st_area()`. Nothing in R evaluates it: `dbplyr` captures the name and sends it as text, and the server resolves it. Attaching `sf` changes nothing, and detaching it changes nothing. The same expression below `collect()` is the `sf` function, and above it is the server's.

A name the server does not have fails loudly, with `UNRESOLVED_ROUTINE`, whether it is a typo or a real `sf` function with no server equivalent. That is the safe case, and it is not the one to plan around.

The case to plan around is a name that exists on both sides and does not mean the same thing, because that runs cleanly and answers wrongly. Twenty-two names are in that position. It comes in three kinds, and all three are live on this page:

- **A number that is wrong by a factor of a hundred thousand.** Ask the server for a distance or an area on longitude and latitude and you get degrees where `sf` would give you metres. [The section below](#the-earth-is-round-in-sf-and-flat-on-the-server) works it through.
- **A true-or-false test that is wrong for a few rows.** `st_contains()` and its relatives agree with `sf` in the middle of a polygon and disagree on its edge. This is the one that will cost you time, because a join off by four rows out of thirteen thousand does not look like anything.
- **A different return shape.** `st_contains()` gives one boolean per row on the server and a sparse index list in `sf`; `st_distance()` gives a scalar per row against a matrix; `st_buffer()` takes two arguments and rejects `sf`'s `nQuadSegs`. This one is porting friction rather than a trap: you will see it immediately. [Which spatial functions you have](../ref/spatial-functions.qmd#where-the-semantics-differ-from-sf) tabulates them.

The first two have a single cause and a single fix, which is the next section. Note what the first two have in common: nothing warns you, and both answers are defensible. You will not find these by reading the error log, because there is no error.

So the position of `collect()` is not a stylistic detail in a spatial pipeline: it decides which implementation of a shared name you get. When you are unsure which side you are on, `show_query()` settles it, and anything it shows you is the server's.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
catalog <- Sys.getenv("DATABRICKS_CATALOG")
schema <- Sys.getenv("DATABRICKS_SCHEMA")

  odbc::databricks(),
  httpPath = Sys.getenv("DATABRICKS_PATH"),
  DefaultStringColumnLength = 65535
)

acon <- dbConnect(
  brickster::DatabricksSQL(),
  warehouse_id = basename(Sys.getenv("DATABRICKS_PATH"))
)

catchments <- tbl(con, in_catalog(catalog, schema, "wfd_catchments"))

catchments |>
  filter(!is.na(geom_wkb)) |>
  mutate(g = st_setsrid(st_geomfromwkb(geom_wkb), 27700L)) |>
  summarise(
    n_catchments = n(),
    area_km2 = round(sum(st_area(g), na.rm = TRUE) / 1e6)
  ) |>
  collect()
```

```
# A tibble: 1 × 2
  n_catchments area_km2
       <int64>    <dbl>
1         4080   130229
```
:::


How many exactly depends on the compute, and not in the direction you would guess. There were 97 on a Pro warehouse running serverless when this was measured, and 93 on an all-purpose cluster. `st_makepoint()`, `st_makeenvelope()`, `st_pointonsurface()` and `st_collect()` are the four missing from the cluster. So the larger, more expensive compute has the smaller spatial vocabulary. If you need a point from two numbers on a cluster, `st_point()` works on both and does the same job. The older Classic warehouse type is a third case, where the functions are documented as unavailable, per function rather than anywhere you would find it by browsing.

Ninety-seven is a lot, and it is still not all of `sf`. The absences worth knowing before you plan around them are `st_makevalid()`, `st_relate()`, `st_voronoi()`, `st_snap()`, `st_segmentize()`, `st_sample()`, `st_polygonize()` and `st_shortestline()`. `st_makevalid()` is the one likely to stop you, because repairing an invalid geometry is a routine step in `sf` and there is no server-side equivalent: the server will tell you a polygon is invalid with `st_isvalid()` and will not fix it. Repair before loading, or collect and repair in R.

That leaves you one ambiguous error to interpret. A function that does not exist on your compute fails with the same message as a name you misspelled, differing only in the name it quotes, so it cannot tell you which mistake you made. Check the spelling and the compute together, because the platform will not separate them for you. A wrong number of arguments is the easy case, and does produce a distinguishable error naming how many the function wanted.

## Set the CRS yourself

The polygons are stored as WKB in a `BINARY` column, and WKB carries no SRID. Ask the server what coordinate system the stored bytes are in and it says zero, meaning it does not know:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
catchments |>
  filter(!is.na(geom_wkb)) |>
  transmute(
    water_body_id,
    srid = st_srid(st_geomfromwkb(geom_wkb))
  ) |>
  head(3) |>
  collect()
```

```
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  water_body_id   srid
  <chr>          <int>
1 GB105035046170     0
2 GB109055036620     0
3 GB112069061390     0
```
:::


The number has to come from you. For this data it is EPSG:27700, the British National Grid, because that is what the Environment Agency publishes. `st_setsrid()` asserts it server-side and `st_set_crs()` asserts it in R. Neither reprojects anything: they attach a label to coordinates that already had that meaning.

Skip it and the two sides fail differently, which is the part worth knowing before you pick where to work. R computes anyway. Decode a polygon, ask for its area without declaring anything, and you get numbers with no CRS, no warning and nothing wrong-looking about them:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
rows <- tbl(acon, in_catalog(catalog, schema, "wfd_catchments")) |>
  filter(!is.na(geom_wkb)) |>
  select(geom_wkb) |>
  head(3) |>
  collect()
```

Those areas happen to be right, because the stored coordinates are already metres. Feed the same CRS-less geometry to anything that needs to know where on Earth it is, though, and the silence ends: a distance in degrees, a join against a layer in another projection, a transform. The answer is wrong or absent and nothing says which.

The server is stricter, and its strictness is a gift here. It refuses rather than guessing. Ask it to transform geometry whose SRID it does not know, and nothing happens at all:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
catchments |>
  filter(!is.na(geom_wkb)) |>
  transmute(g = st_transform(st_geomfromwkb(geom_wkb), 27700L)) |>
  head(1) |>
  collect()
```

So the habit to build is to wrap `st_geomfromwkb()` in `st_setsrid()` every time, in the `mutate()` that first decodes the bytes, and never let an un-labelled geometry reach the verbs downstream of it.

Necessary, though, is not sufficient, and this is the point at which it would be reasonable to think the CRS problem is solved. It is not: labelling the coordinates does not make the server measure them the way `sf` would. The next section is the part that bites.

## The Earth is round in `sf`, and flat on the server

Setting the CRS is necessary and not sufficient. There is a second divergence underneath it that no error will ever tell you about, and it is the one most likely to end up in a paper.

You already know that a distance on a sphere is not a distance on a flat map. The trap is that `sf` and Databricks make opposite default choices about it, and the same line of code gets whichever choice belongs to the side it ran on.

Since version 1.0, `sf` treats longitude and latitude as points on a sphere. Hand it unprojected coordinates and it uses s2 spherical geometry and returns metres. The server does the opposite: it discards the coordinate system entirely and does flat arithmetic on the raw numbers, so on longitude and latitude it is doing plane geometry on degrees. Neither is a bug. They are two defensible answers to two different questions, and the pipeline gives you no clue which one you asked.

Here is the size of it, both sides computed side by side. Two points a nominal five degrees apart:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
server <- dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT st_distance(a, b)       AS planar,
         st_distancesphere(a, b) AS sphere
  FROM (SELECT st_geomfromtext('POINT(0 0)', 4326) AS a,
               st_geomfromtext('POINT(3 4)', 4326) AS b)
")

in_r <- st_distance(
  st_sfc(st_point(c(0, 0)), crs = 4326),
  st_sfc(st_point(c(3, 4)), crs = 4326)
)

tibble(
  asked = c("server, st_distance", "server, st_distancesphere", "sf, in R"),
  answer = c(server$planar, server$sphere, as.numeric(in_r))
)
```

```
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  asked                      answer
  <chr>                       <dbl>
1 server, st_distance            5 
2 server, st_distancesphere 555813.
3 sf, in R                  555813.
```
:::


Five against half a million. The server's `5` is the separation in degrees, computed correctly. `sf`'s figure is the same separation in metres, also computed correctly. Nothing warns, both look like plausible numbers, and if the units are not printed next to them there is nothing to notice.

The quieter half of the same problem is that true-or-false tests diverge too, and only on boundaries. Take a unit square and a point sitting exactly on the middle of its bottom edge. On the server the point is on the edge, because the edge is a straight line from (0,0) to (1,0). In `sf` the edge is a geodesic that bows away from that straight line, so the point is genuinely not on it. `st_intersects()`, `st_covers()` and `st_touches()` come back TRUE on the server and FALSE in `sf`, and `st_disjoint()` the other way round. Points well inside and well outside the polygon agree on both sides.

That asymmetry is what makes it expensive. A spatial join puts its ambiguous records exactly on boundaries, so the rows that disagree are the ones you would have wanted to look at. Your overflow count is four out of thirteen thousand different from what R would have said, both numbers are defensible, and nothing in the output suggests you should check.

So do not carry away "measurements are risky, true-or-false tests are safe". It is a natural summary and it is wrong.

### The fix is to project, and the tempting alternatives are worse

Project your coordinates before you ask a spatial question, and both problems disappear at once.

The reason it works on both sides is worth holding onto: `sf` reaches for spherical geometry only when the data is unprojected. Give it a projected CRS and it does flat arithmetic on a plane, which is what the server was doing all along. The two models coincide, and every case tested agreed exactly.

This data is stored in EPSG:27700, already projected into metres, which is why the areas earlier on this page can be trusted and why the join at the foot of it is sound. Had the catchments been stored in longitude and latitude, that same `st_area()` call would have returned square degrees and the numbers would have looked like a unit mistake nobody made.

Five things look like fixes and are not. Three of them are the obvious things to try:

- **Attaching `sf`.** The generic is never called, so it changes nothing. Nor does detaching it.
- **Tagging the SRID.** `st_setsrid()` is still worth doing, for the reasons in the section above, but `st_distance()` ignores it. "The column has a CRS" does not mean the measurement respected it.
- **Changing connection path.** `odbc`, `brickster` and `sparklyr` were each measured, and all three return the same wrong answer just as silently. There is nothing to choose between them here.

The fourth is that nothing can warn you. Whether a call is wrong depends on the CRS of the data, and `dbplyr` writes the SQL before anything has asked the server what it is holding, so no automatic check can decide at that point. This one is yours to get right.

The fifth is the one to be most careful about, because it is what an experienced `sf` user reaches for first. **`sf_use_s2(FALSE)` is a trap.** It switches `sf` to an ellipsoidal model, not a flat one. That repairs the boundary disagreement, so the true-or-false tests start matching and it looks as though it worked, while the measurements stay wrong by five orders of magnitude. You have removed the symptom you could have found and kept the one you could not. Leave s2 alone and project instead.

If you specifically want a distance on a sphere from unprojected coordinates, ask the server for it by name. `st_distancesphere()` and `st_distancespheroid()` do that, as the comparison above shows: the difference between the two is the sphere against the ellipsoid, which is the ordinary choice you already make in `sf`.

The geography type is the other route and it is not a drop-in. `st_distance()` refuses a geography argument outright with a datatype mismatch, so you cannot fix a flat answer by casting the input: use the functions just named, or work in geography throughout with `st_length()` and `st_area()`, which do accept it. Geography is also still Public Preview where the geometry type is generally available, which is worth knowing before you build on it.

Mixing two coordinate systems is the good case by comparison: that fails loudly, as [the section above](#set-the-crs-yourself) shows. This one does not fail at all.

One caveat on the twenty-two overlapping names. That was counted once, against one runtime and one version of `sf`, so treat it as an observation rather than a promise. The modelling difference underneath it is documented behaviour on both sides and will outlast the count.

## Transforming once, server-side, instead of per iteration

`st_transform()` works server-side, so a reprojection can happen once, in the query, rather than in R on every pass of an analysis. The storm overflow locations are longitude and latitude, EPSG:4326, and the catchments are EPSG:27700, so something has to move before the two layers can meet:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tbl(con, in_catalog(catalog, schema, "storm_overflows")) |>
  filter(!is.na(longitude)) |>
  mutate(p = st_transform(st_point(longitude, latitude, 4326L), 27700L)) |>
  transmute(
    overflow_id,
    easting = round(st_x(p), 1),
    northing = round(st_y(p), 1)
  ) |>
  head(3) |>
  collect()
```

```
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  overflow_id easting northing
  <chr>         <dbl>    <dbl>
1 SVT00708    384585.  205042.
2 SVT00753    434509.  347118.
3 SVT01386    388700.  250259.
```
:::


Note that `st_point()` takes the SRID as its third argument, which is what makes the transform legal. The same rule as above: say what the coordinates are before asking anything to move them.

This transform is doing two jobs, and the second is easy to miss. The layers have to share a coordinate system before they can meet, which is the obvious one. It also moves the overflows out of longitude and latitude before any predicate touches them, which is what makes the join at the foot of this page agree with the answer `sf` would give. Reprojecting to suit the join is the same act as reprojecting for correctness, so this pattern is worth keeping even when both layers already match.

## Aggregating server-side when only a scalar needs to cross

This is the best case on the site, and the shape to look for in your own analysis: the geometry stays where it is, the spatial work happens there, and a small table comes back.

Group by an ordinary column while aggregating the geometry. Here that is ecological class, six values, with the catchments in each class unioned and the union's area measured:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
catchments |>
  filter(!is.na(geom_wkb), !is.na(ecological_class)) |>
  mutate(g = st_setsrid(st_geomfromwkb(geom_wkb), 27700L)) |>
  group_by(ecological_class) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    area_km2 = round(st_area(st_union_agg(g)) / 1e6)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(area_km2)) |>
  collect()
```

```
# A tibble: 6 × 3
  ecological_class       n area_km2
  <chr>            <int64>    <dbl>
1 Moderate            2208    74367
2 Poor                 710    23266
3 Good                 512    14089
4 Not assessed         219     4831
5 Bad                  119     4044
6 High                   4       76
```
:::


Six rows crossed. The 27 MB of polygons behind them did not.

You may have read that geometry cannot take part in grouped queries. The restriction is much narrower than that reads. Grouping by an ordinary key while aggregating geometry works, as above, and so does grouping by something derived from the geometry such as a geohash. What fails is grouping by a geometry column itself, because the type has no ordering. The error says exactly that and names the column:

```
✖  (80) Syntax or semantic analysis error thrown in server while
  executing query. Error message from server:
  org.apache.spark.sql.catalyst.ExtendedAnalysisException: The
  expression "g" cannot be used as a grouping e
```

So the pattern is not blocked, only one spelling of it is, and the one you want is the spelling that works.

## The full `sf` pipeline below the line, when that is what you want

Bringing the polygons back is a legitimate answer, not a defeat. If the geometry fits in your session and you have an `sf` pipeline already written, collecting it is the right call: you get the whole of `sf` rather than the subset the server exposes, and you are working in an idiom you already know.

The connection caveat decides how. Geometry cannot travel over the ODBC path, because `odbc` silently returns only part of a `BINARY` value, so this route needs `brickster::DatabricksSQL()`. See [Connect your R session to the data](connect.qmd) for why, and for the check that the bytes arrived whole.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
catchment_sf <- tbl(acon, in_catalog(catalog, schema, "wfd_catchments")) |>
  filter(!is.na(geom_wkb)) |>
  select(water_body_id, ecological_class, water_body_area_m2, geom_wkb) |>
  collect() |>
  mutate(
    geometry = st_as_sfc(structure(geom_wkb, class = "WKB"),
                         EWKB = TRUE) |>
      st_set_crs(27700)
  ) |>
  select(-geom_wkb) |>
  st_as_sf()
```

The server-side route earns its complexity when the geometry is large and the answer is small, not when both are small.

## Points work the same way

Nothing above is specific to polygons. Points get the same treatment, and the predicate join runs server-side too. Counting storm overflows inside catchments, grouped by the catchment's ecological class, takes both layers, transforms one of them and returns five rows.

One wrinkle: `join_by()` accepts only equality and a few range helpers, so a spatial predicate cannot be written as the join condition. Pair the two tables with `cross_join()` and filter on the predicate instead. That reads as though every catchment is about to be compared with every overflow, and the query planner does not execute it that way: the filter becomes the join condition, exactly as it would have been in SQL.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
overflows <- tbl(con, in_catalog(catalog, schema, "storm_overflows")) |>
  mutate(p = st_transform(st_point(longitude, latitude, 4326L), 27700L))

catchments |>
  filter(!is.na(ecological_class)) |>
  mutate(g = st_setsrid(st_geomfromwkb(geom_wkb), 27700L)) |>
  cross_join(overflows) |>
  filter(st_contains(g, p)) |>
  count(ecological_class, name = "n_overflows") |>
  arrange(desc(n_overflows)) |>
  collect()
```

```
# A tibble: 5 × 2
  ecological_class n_overflows
  <chr>                <int64>
1 Moderate                8491
2 Poor                    2027
3 Good                     547
4 Not assessed             436
5 Bad                      276
```
:::


Both SRIDs are asserted inside the join condition, and that is not decoration: `st_contains()` refuses two arguments with different SRIDs rather than assuming they match.

Both layers are also in EPSG:27700 by the time the predicate sees them, and that is what makes this count trustworthy rather than approximately right. Had the overflows still been in longitude and latitude, this join would have run without complaint and disagreed with `sf` on every point sitting on a catchment boundary, which on a layer of catchments that share their edges is not a rare case. The transform is load-bearing, not tidiness.

Reading the overflow data here is subject to its own licence, which is CC BY 4.0 and not the Open Government Licence that covers the rest.

The worked example does this same join the other way, in `sf` after collecting both layers, and then checks the two answers against each other. See [The spatial join](../example/spatial.qmd) if you want the comparison rather than the recipe.

## Next

Gridded data does not work like this. The `ST_` functions are vector functions with no raster equivalent, so [work with rasters](terra.qmd) inverts everything on this page: there is no server-side path, and the work comes to you. And if you want to confirm the server-side answer matches R's, see [Check that you get the same answer wherever it ran](check-the-answer.qmd).

---
